title: PGA Tour season headed for Monday finish after rain washes out Saturday at RSM Classic
article_text:
The 2026 PGA Tour season will last one day longer than expected.

With pouring rain pummeling St. Simons Island, Georgia, the third round of the season-ending RSM Classic was postponed until Sunday. The final round will be played on Monday. It will be the PGA Tour’s third Monday finish of the fall slate.

“Obviously this is seaside golf, the golf course is very flat, the fairways are generally very flat with just a little bit of subtle movement,” PGA Tour chief referee Steve Rintoul told reporters on Saturday about the decision not to play on Saturday. “They’re above the marsh; they’re not sand-based. Even though it’s sea level, a dunes links look here, it’s not sand-based. So we had a lot of water sitting on the surface, especially in pockets in low areas in fairways where, I mentioned earlier, [we] may have a player who’s in the fairway in temporary water and needs to take relief, and that nearest point of relief takes him outside of the fairway. That takes the preferred lies out of his hands, and it just becomes, it’s not equitable when we get to that. So that kind of forced our hand.”

After 36 holes, Michael Thorbjorsen, Marco Penge and Rasmus Neegaard-Petersen are tied atop the leaderboard at 9 under. Six players, including Haotong Li and Rasmus Hojgaard, are one shot back.

The RSM Classic is the final event of the PGA Tour’s FedEx Cup Fall season, meaning it’s the last chance for players outside of the top 100 to move inside that number to keep their full-time playing privileges.

There has already been plenty of heartbreak at the RSM Classic.

John Parry, who entered the week at 96 in the FedEx Cup rankings, three-putted his final hole on Friday to miss the cut. He is now projected to finish the year at 101. Billy Horschel shot 71-74 to miss the cut and is projected to finish at 105. Tony Finau shot 71-71 to miss the cut and is projected to finish at 119.

Three weeks ago at the Butterfield Bermuda Championship, high winds forced the PGA Tour to call the tournament final after 54 holes and hold a sudden-death playoff on Monday between Austin Smotherman and Seamus Power. With so much on the line this week and a good forecast on the horizon, the PGA Tour does not anticipate the same at the RSM Classic.

“The situation here is very different than the situation we had in Bermuda where high winds were forecast, and there was no physical way they were going to be able to play on Monday,” Rintoul said. “In fact, they had to choose one hole to play that playoff, but there was no physical way they were going to play that. Then the regulations also give the option at that point to reduce the tournament to 54 holes, which they did. Here we have a good forecast, and using the regulations, we’ll play 72 holes even if that means extending into Monday.”

The PGA Tour season has 36 holes left. And after a Saturday washout, it’s headed for a drama-filled Monday finish.

title: RSM Classic Set For Monday Finish After Saturday Washout
article_text:
The RSM Classic title - and the hopes of PGA Tour pros battling to secure full playing privileges for 2027 - will not be decided until Monday.

Because of “unplayable course conditions” at Sea Island's Seaside Course, no play was possible on Saturday, meaning the third round will now be played on Sunday, with the final round set for Monday.

A statement from the PGA Tour read: "Due to unplayable course conditions at Sea Island Golf Club resulting from inclement weather today, the third round of The RSM Classic will be contested on Sunday, November 22, with the final round to be played on Monday, November 23."

"Third-round tee times on Sunday will run from 9:10-11 a.m. ET off Nos. 1 and 10 in groups of three. Final-round tee times on Monday are projected to run from 7:20-9:10 a.m. ET off Nos. 1 and 10 in groups of three."

Meanwhile, it has also been confirmed that only Sunday tickets will be accepted for the third round, and there will be no spectators for the final round on Monday.

Some of the field experienced downpours during Friday's second round, and there were more warning signs that Saturday's play could face disruption when rain fell overnight in the area.

That led to the start of the third round initially being delayed, with the hope that play could begin after 10.30am local time.

However, at around 12.45pm local time, the announcement came that no play would be possible on Saturday.

The decision means that there will be a Monday finish on the PGA Tour for the second consecutive week, the first time that has happened since 2015.

At the Austin Championship, the final round was delayed until Monday due to inclement weather, ensuring no play was possible on Sunday.

Eventually, Chad Ramey held off Ben Kohles to win by two shots.

As well as the drama associated with that battle, it also means a day of frustration for those challenging for the title.

title: Rick Shiels hits back after catching strays from LIV Golf’s Chief Restructuring Officer
article_text:
Rick Shiels has hit back after finding himself on the receiving end of criticism from LIV Golf’s Chief Restructuring Officer David Orlofsky amid the collapse of LIV Golf.

Shiels is one of the most recognisable figures in golf content creation, with over 3 million subscribers to his YouTube channel.

Such is his influence in the game, Shiels took part in the Internet Invitational this year which featured 64 content creators competing for $4m.

It appeared, however, according to Front Office Sports' David Rumsey, that Orlofsky didn’t know who Shiels was when discussing those that are owed money by LIV Golf.

“As I understand it, Rick Shiels is some sort of golf influencer, but I have never heard of him,” he said when asked why he Englishman was owed $1.4m.

“So I couldn’t tell you much about him, but apparently his job was to write stuff and publicise stuff about the events. And because he has supposedly a following, people were supposed to – there’s supposed to be some value he added there. I couldn’t pick him out of a lineup.”

The $1.4m figure is what Shiels is due from the league after signing up in January 2025 on a multi-year strategic partnership as an official ambassador and content creator.

Those comments from Orlofsky are particular tone deaf, especially considering Shiels wasn’t hired to write content.

The Englishman has finally responded, however.

Shiels has established himself over the years as one of golf’s biggest and most influential content creators, especially on this side of the Atlantic.

He has played with the likes of Sir Nick Faldo and Tom Watson, while interviewing countless names in the world of professional golf through his YouTube channel.

The 40-year-old was unwilling to let the comments from Orlofsky pass though as he took to Instagram to offer his own thoughts.

“Unbelievable” replied Shiels on Ziregolf’s Instagram page stating that Orlofsky didn’t know who Shiels was, adding in a laughing face emoji.

“David who?” the Englishman also stated and it shows just how much of a fallout the collapse of LIV Golf has caused, as it isn’t just Shiels who is owed money.

Indeed, the BBC reports that the R&A are still due £500k from the Saudi-backed league, whole smaller business are also waiting on money.

“This consultancy support will help elevate conditions across the league’s 14-event season, spanning ten countries and five continents.” read an R&A statement at the time.

Elsewhere, Global Infusion Group is still due £321,671 for catering services provided at the LIV Golf UK event back in July, while cleaning company BD365 Clean are owed £75,225 for providing 108 members of staff.

Overall, creditors have submitted more than £100m in unsecured claims throughout the bankruptcy process, yet LIV has put aside just £2m to deal with those recoveries.

The numbers simply don't add up and it remains to be seen whether Shiels, or any other person/company due money by LIV will ever see a penny.

Shiels’ role during his time with LIV Golf was to spend time with each team, filming videos while bringing back his old ‘break 75’ series to showcase the league and its players.

He did previously withdraw a claim for $7,040,700 against LIV Golf Incorporated, which is separate from the $1.4m he is currently owed.

There will surely be plenty more twists and turns in this ongoing saga, no doubt about that. For Shiels, though, it is clear he isn’t one to back down from a fight given his recent replies to Orlofsky.

title: Jon Rahm Handed Major PGA Tour Update After LIV Golf Collapse
article_text:
Jon Rahm's future in professional golf remains uncertain following his departure from LIV Golf. The Spaniard has already secured a place on the DP World Tour for the 2027 season, but his PGA Tour status remains unresolved. His next move could have major implications for his career as he looks to return to the American circuit.

The former world No. 1 joined LIV Golf in December 2023, signing a lucrative deal that reportedly valued around $300 million. However, disagreements over the league's proposed changes and its future direction led to his departure.

With LIV Golf's collapse changing the landscape of professional golf, Rahm is now waiting for clarity on his next chapter.

Jon Rahm could soon receive a clearer picture of his PGA Tour future, with officials expected to discuss his potential reinstatement during the first week of December.

According to Ten Golf, the meeting could determine whether the two-time major champion has a pathway back to the American circuit for the 2027 season.

Rahm said he knew nothing about the PGA Tour's plans for his return. After the DP World Tour Championship, he said the decision rested with Tour leaders and their upcoming meetings.

"I imagine they have their boards, their meetings to hold for whatever is coming at the end of the year, and I imagine one of those points will be me. I just don't know if it'll be this November or December. I have no idea," Rahm told Ten Golf.

The reported December discussion could matter to Rahm, who has expressed interest in returning to the PGA Tour.

But reinstatement terms remain unclear, and the Tour has announced no new framework, leaving the Spaniard awaiting an official decision.

Rahm has previously indicated he would accept conditions similar to those imposed on Brooks Koepka when he returned earlier this year.

Brooks Koepka remains an important reference point for Rahm's potential return.

The five-time major champion was the only player to accept the PGA Tour's Returning Member Program after the offer was also extended to Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith.

Koepka's reinstatement required a $5 million charitable contribution and the forfeiture of potential participation in the PGA Tour Player Equity Program from 2026 to 2030.

The Tour estimated the value of those lost equity opportunities at approximately $50 million to $85 million.

Rahm has suggested that he would be open to accepting comparable terms if the opportunity became available.

Meanwhile, PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp confirmed on November 16 that the organization's boards had discussed the possibility of former LIV Golf players returning.

"We engaged in thoughtful discussion on the topic of LIV players with both boards today," Rolapp said.

He also said more information could come at the beginning of the new year.

However, the one-year exclusion rule could delay Rahm's eligibility until August 2027 unless the Tour changes or waives it.

The December meeting could therefore determine not only whether Rahm is welcomed back, but also what conditions he must meet before returning to competition.

title: YouTube Star Peter Finch Confirmed For DP World Tour Debut
article_text:
Golf content creator Peter Finch has revealed he will make his DP World Tour debut at next month’s AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open.

Finch, a Golf Monthly Top 50 coach with over 851,000 subscribers on YouTube, announced the news on Instagram.

He wrote: “I’m thrilled to share that I will be teeing it up at the AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open on the @dpworldtour.”

He added: “I cannot wait to get out to Mauritius and compete against some of the best players in the world!”

Finch also published a video, where he said he was “elated to be living a childhood dream.”

He described the event, which will take place at Mont Choisy Le Golf, as “the most beautiful week in the calendar year on the DP World Tour.”

He added: “I remember watching this tournament over the years and just thinking what an amazing spectacle and an amazing privilege it would be to play at these courses and that’s what we’re going to be doing.”

Finch, who also confirmed he will be making content at the event, invited fans to comment on whether he could make the cut.

If he’s seeking inspiration for that challenge, he can get if from his Asian Development Tour debut at the Egyptian Open in 2025.

On that occasion, he made the cut on the way to placing T50. Earlier in 2025, Finch made Final Qualifying for The Open, although he fell short in his bid for his maiden Major appearance.

He also has had some success in 2026, finishing T6 at the Fairmont St Andrews Classic on the Tartan Pro Tour.

The DP World Tour represents a significant step up in quality from both circuits, as demonstrated by the respective tournaments' field ratings.

A tournament's field rating measures the overall strength of its line-up, based on the quality of the players competing.

The 2025 Egyptian Open had a field rating of 6.10, while this year’s field rating for the Fairmont St Andrews Classic was 3.05.

For comparison, the field rating for the 2025 AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open was 82.59.

Jayden Schaper won the tournament a year ago, beating Ryan Gerard in a playoff, a result that helped him become one of 10 players to earn a PGA Tour card via the 2026 Race to Dubai ranking.

Other former winners of the event include Louis Oosthuizen, Rasmus Hojgaard and Kurt Kitayama.

Finch is far from the first golf content creator to test himself at the highest level.

One example is Good Good Golf’s Brad Dalke, who played in the DP World Tour event, the BMW International Open this year, challenging for the title before finishing T30.

title: Pro's disaster 3-putt costs him full PGA Tour card
article_text:
We’re only halfway through the final PGA Tour event of the year, where players are fighting for PGA Tour status for next season. But the carnage is already apparent.

Look no further than the case of John Parry.

The 40-year-old entered the RSM Classic near the bubble for fully exempt PGA Tour status. On Friday, he was in line to make the cut and keep the fight going over the weekend, until a disastrous three-putt on his closing hole cost him the cut and, likely, his full PGA Tour card.

While there are a lot of permutations for PGA Tour status on the line at the RSM Classic, arguably the most impactful is the top-100 cutoff.

All players who finish within the top 100 of the FedEx Fall standings at the end of the tournament receive fully exempt status on the PGA Tour in 2027, as well as a spot in the Players Championship.

While that doesn’t necessarily mean they get access to next year’s Signature Events, at the very least, their playing schedules will be secure for a year, and they can play their way into the bigger events.

Parry is technically a rookie, having earned his 2026 PGA Tour card via the DP World Tour’s Race to Dubai last season. But he’s well aware of the top-100 cutoff.

Heading into the RSM Classic, Parry was stuck at 96th in the FedEx Fall standings. Though that’s not much of a cushion, the veteran pro would have likely needed only to make the cut at Sea Island to stay within the top 100.

Following an opening-round 70, Parry started Friday’s second round right on what would end up being the cut line: two under. A birdie at the Seaside Course’s second hole moved him to three under.

But then things got shaky. Parry made bogeys at 3 and 5, then two more at 13 and 14 to fall to one over. Incredibly, he then rallied with birdies at 15 and 17 to move back to one under.

As he headed to the 18th tee, the cut line still hovered at one under, meaning he only needed a par to play the weekend.

Parry striped his drive into the middle of the fairway, then knocked his approach to 29 feet. At the time, he believed a two-putt par would give him a made cut.

Unfortunately, he’d need more than two to finish out.

Parry’s birdie putt ran 3 feet, 10 inches past the hole. Then he lined up his par putt and pulled it just left of the hole, watching his ball nip the edge but fail to fall. A tap-in gave him a devastating bogey-5.

With his ugly finish, Parry had temporarily dropped to 99th in the FedEx Fall standings, which means he was still in line for a full PGA Tour card. But by round’s end, the cut line moved to two under, and Parry fell to 101st in the FedEx Fall standings.

There is some good news for Parry. Even though he likely won’t be fully exempt for 2027 as a result of his missed cut, he will still finish within the top 110, which will give him conditional PGA Tour status for next year and plenty of starts.

title: Haeran Ryu Opens With Bogey-Free 66 at CME Group Tour Championship
article_text:
Megan McCrea is the Manager of Digital Operations. Megan is in her second year with the LPGA, working with the LPGA and Epson Tours to manage, develop, maintain, and update website content.

NAPLES, Fla. — Haeran Ryu of the Republic of Korea carded a bogey-free 6-under 66 on Thursday to sit T4 after the first round of the CME Group Tour Championship, one shot behind co-leaders Jeeno Thitikul, A Lim Kim and Karis Davidson at Tiburón Golf Club.

The 25-year-old, who won the KPMG Women's PGA Championship and The Amundi Evian Championship in back-to-back starts this summer, closed with birdies on her final two holes to join eight other players at 6-under. The 66 is Ryu's lowest score in 13 career rounds at the season-ending event, where her previous best was a second-round 67 in 2025.

Thitikul, the two-time defending champion, A Lim Kim and Davidson each opened with 7-under 65s on the par-72 Gold Course, leaving a crowded leaderboard with three rounds to play.

Ryu started on the front nine and wasted no time, making birdie on the par-5 first hole to reach 1-under. She parred her next four holes before picking up another stroke at the par-5 sixth to move to 2-under, then added three more pars to turn in 2-under 34.

The back nine is where Ryu found another gear. After a par at the 10th, she birdied the par-4 11th to get to 3-under and followed with a birdie at the par-4 13th to climb to 4-under.

A run of three straight pars followed, including at the par-5 14th, the only par 5 she did not birdie on the day. Ryu then finished with a flourish, making back-to-back birdies at the par-5 17th and the par-4 18th to post an inward 32 and move within one shot of the lead.

In all, Ryu made six birdies and 12 pars, playing the four par 5s in 3-under and never dropping a shot.

Ryu credited a simple game plan for keeping a clean card, one that included taking cues from Thitikul, who has won this event each of the last two years.

“Today I just had two strategies on the golf course. First one, just not think about the golf course; just more control my swing,” said Ryu. “And second one is Jeeno is a pretty good player on this golf course, and I just wanted to follow her.”

Ryu admitted Florida has not always been kind to her. As a rookie in 2023, she tied for 36th in her first start at Tiburón.

“My first year I was a rookie, and Florida was not a good memory for me, so that’s why I need more experience on the golf course in Florida,” said Ryu. “But these days, way better than before.”

Ryu’s six-birdie effort continued a strong close to her season. She shot a 6-under 65 in difficult conditions on Saturday at The ANNIKA driven by Gainbridge at Pelican last week on her way to a T3 finish, and she was T2 at the BMW Ladies Championship in October.

It has been a breakthrough year for the 2023 Rolex Rookie of the Year. Ryu has 12 top-10 finishes in 17 starts in 2026 and has earned $4.9 million. She captured her first major title at the KPMG Women's PGA Championship at Hazeltine National Golf Club in June, then won The Amundi Evian Championship two weeks later in a playoff over Brooke Henderson. Her third-round 60 at Evian was the lowest score in LPGA major championship history.

Ryu entered the week third in the Race to CME Globe standings. She owns five career LPGA Tour titles: the 2023 Walmart NW Arkansas Championship, the 2024 FM Championship, the 2025 Black Desert Championship and her two 2026 majors.

This is Ryu's fourth appearance at the CME Group Tour Championship. She tied for 36th at 9-under as a rookie in 2023, tied for 35th at 6-under in 2024 and posted her best finish last year, a T10 at 13-under. Her previous opening rounds here were 69, 71 and 69 respectively.

With 54 holes remaining and a $4 million first prize on the line, Ryu is in position to add a third victory to her 2026 season. The path will not be easy. Twelve players are within one shot of the lead, and Race to CME Globe leader Nelly Korda opened with a 4-under 68 to sit T20.

Ryu said her approach for the rest of the week will not change.

“I just want to keep not thinking about the golf course and just want to keep patient in my swing,” said Ryu. “That’s it. Nothing more.”

Haeran tees off during second round of the CME Group Tour Championship at 11:55 a.m Friday.

title: Thitikul, Kim and Davidson share CME Group Tour Championship lead
article_text:
The LPGA Tour's season finale has a crowded leaderboard after the first day. Jeeno Thitikul, A Lim Kim and Karis Davidson each opened the CME Group Tour Championship at Tiburón Golf Club with a 7-under-par 65. They share the lead at -7, one stroke ahead of a nine-player group at -6. With three rounds still to play, very little separates the top of the 60-player field.

Thitikul is the most closely watched of the three co-leaders. The world No. 2 won this event in 2024 and 2025 and arrived in Naples trying to win the Tour Championship for a third year in a row. Her bogey-free-looking start of seven under puts her right in contention, although that bid is still three rounds away from being decided. A Lim Kim of South Korea and Karis Davidson of Australia matched her score, so the opening round produced a three-nation tie between Thailand, Korea and Australia.

Charley Hull is the best-known name in the group one shot back. The Englishwoman won this event in 2016 and shot a 6-under 66 that included seven birdies, missing only one fairway. She said she had struggled with her swing early in the round: "I felt like I had no swing feels. Then as the round developed, I hit it really nice." Looking back a decade, Hull joked: "It's crazy how long ago it was and how chubby I was back then." Her opening round continues a solid run of form: she has five consecutive top-25 finishes, including a tie for 17th at the previous week's event.

Eight other players are tied with Hull at -6, and Korea has the most of them. Hye Jin Choi, Somi Lee and Haeran Ryu all shot 66. So did Americans Lauren Coughlin, Jenny Bae and Auston Kim, Japan's Ayaka Furue and France's Pauline Roussin-Bouchard.

Another seven players are two shots off the lead at -5 after rounds of 67. They include Frenchwoman Celine Boutier and England's Lottie Woad, along with Australia's Grace Kim, Mexico's Gaby Lopez, Japan's Yuna Nishimura, American Yealimi Noh and China's Yan Liu.

The group at -4 is also within reach. It includes Spain's Carlota Ciganda, Australia's Hannah Green, Korea's Ina Yoon and Germany's Esther Henseleit. Henseleit's 68 leaves her three shots behind the leaders and in a good position to move up over the next three days.

Thirty players are within three strokes of the lead, so the opening round has settled very little. Low scores were common on Thursday, and anyone in the top 20 can expect to stay in contention with another good round. The second round on Friday should start to separate the field before the weekend. For now, Thitikul, Kim and Davidson are the players to catch, and a large group is close behind them.

title: LPGA Tour introduce ‘aggressive’ new solution to stop slow play
article_text:
The LPGA Tour is tackling pace of play head-on.

It's one of the biggest issues fans have with the modern game, as players are often taking around six hours to complete their rounds. And while the PGA Tour has often been criticized for not taking action to speed up the pace of play, the LPGA Tour is attempting to find solutions.

Their latest move is to fine any player who has been put on the clock over 35 times in a year $35,000. That's an extreme measure, considering the previous threshold was 40 holes, and the previous fine was $5,000.

Under the new policy, the maximum time allowed for a single shot also drops from 70 seconds to 60 seconds, and players will pay $2,000 for a first offense, $4,000 for a second, and $8,000 for a third.

Delays of six to 15 seconds still bring a one-stroke penalty plus a fine, while delays of 16 seconds or more carry a two-stroke penalty and a fine. LPGA Tour Commissioner Craig Kessler explained how the tour came to this new policy.

This new pace-of-play policy is a positive step for the LPGA Tour as it looks to speed up the game, and what's even more encouraging is that the players are also invested in fixing the issue.

How do we know that? Well, the players came up with the solution in the first place. That's according to Kessler, who said on SiriusXM Radio: "The good news is we started with our fans, and the insight from fans is that pace of play matters. Fans want to see us play faster. We brought that to our players, and we actually have a pace-of-play committee.

"And the beautiful thing here is it's the players who developed the policy. They're the ones that we understand the importance of playing faster. We understand what are the levers that we can pull to help bring that to life.

"And they're the ones who created the policy that we rolled out to frankly, a decent amount of applause from our players on Tuesday.

"I'm very excited to see the policy implemented. If it works as intended, fantastic, and of course if we need to learn and adapt as we go then we'll do just that."

This isn't the only step the LPGA Tour has taken. Unlike the PGA Tour, the LPGA has enforced two-stroke penalties on players this season, taking action on Yealimi Noh and Carlota Ciganda and ultimately costing them victories.

Kessler spoke about those instances: "There are two players this season that we have addressed two-stroke penalties to, and they actually lost the tournament on Sunday. And by the way, we didn't do it for that reason, but the reality is, when you've got a policy, if you want players to take that seriously, you have to enforce it.

"Those are tough calls, and sometimes leadership requires you to make unpopular decisions. But I'm proud of our rules team for sticking to the policy we put in place. And for what it's worth, you spend a minute on social and look at the fans' reaction, I think fans are very pleased to see how seriously we're taking this."

The fines likely won't translate into a punishment for the PGA Tour, as they would unfairly affect players who aren't making as much prize money week to week as the biggest stars.

But the PGA Tour can learn from how the LPGA Tour hits players where it hurts: their scorecard. They must follow suit and start docking shots for slow players.

title: Thitikul Stretches Tiburón Streak to Nine Straight Rounds in the 60s
article_text:
A Lim Kim has the lead at the CME Group Tour Championship. But the player behind her is the one who has owned Tiburón Golf Club for the past two years. Jeeno Thitikul has won this event in each of the last two years. On Friday in Naples, Florida, she shot 67 in the second round. That made it nine rounds in a row in the 60s for her at this course, and it keeps her in the race for a third straight title.

Thitikul is alone in second place at 12-under 132, three shots behind A Lim Kim. Kim leads at 15-under 129. Two rounds remain in the LPGA Tour's season finale, so the final weekend of the year now has a clear chase story.

Both players opened with 65 on Thursday. Kim then pulled ahead in the second round, and for a while it looked like she might get well clear. Thitikul answered late. According to golftoday.co.uk, she made five birdies over her last eight holes, which kept the gap to three shots heading into the weekend.

That kind of finish is nothing new for her here. The closing stretch from the 13th to the 18th has been one of her biggest strengths at Tiburón since 2024, and it played a big part in both of her titles. She finished strongly again on Friday, and those late birdies may well matter by Sunday afternoon.

Her run of nine straight rounds in the 60s tells the story of her record here. She does not just play this course well every so often. She shoots in the 60s almost every time she tees it up.

Thitikul still has a lot of ground to make up. Kim's second-round 64 gave her a 36-hole total of 129, the lowest score through two rounds at Tiburón since the event moved to the course in 2013. She birdied all four par-5s, and her round included a hole-in-one at the par-3 16th.

"I needed 155-yard shot, honestly a little strong hit and I make it," Kim said of the ace. "A little luck to me, yeah."

Luck may have helped at 16, but the rest of her round was simply very good golf. A three-shot lead over a two-time defending champion is a strong position. It is not a safe one, though, especially with Thitikul's record here.

The leaderboard is tight below the top two. Six players are tied for third at 11-under 133, just one shot behind Thitikul and four behind Kim:

That leaves Thitikul with a lot of company. If she has a quiet round, someone from that group could easily pass her.

Nelly Korda is at 9-under 135 after rounds of 68 and 67. She was bogey-free on Friday but still lost ground, going from three back after the first round to six back now. That shows how low the leaders went.

The question for Saturday and Sunday is simple. Can Thitikul's record at Tiburón beat Kim's form this week? If Thitikul keeps her streak going, Kim will need to keep scoring low to stay in front. If Kim's game holds up, Thitikul may need something special over the closing holes she knows so well.

title: Gary Woodland Has Knee Surgery, Exits Hero World Challenge
article_text:
Woodland said he had been feeling discomfort in his knee and, after consulting with doctors, had the procedure Thursday night at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York with Dr. Riley Williams, Golf Channel reported.

Keegan Bradley will take Woodland's place in the 20-player field as a tournament invite, Golf Channel and Golfweek reported. The event is Dec. 3-6 at Albany in the Bahamas.

Woodland had received his invitation Tuesday, along with tournament host Tiger Woods and Rickie Fowler, Golfweek reported.

title: Kim moves clear at LPGA finale after hole-in-one
article_text:
South Korea's A-Lim Kim aced the par-three 16th hole on her way to claiming a three-shot lead after the second round of CME Group Tour Championship.

The 31-year-old held a share of the lead after the first round at Tiburon Golf Club in Florida but is out on her own after shooting a superb 64 on Friday.

Kim made seven birdies and one eagle, the hole-in-one on 16, with a solitary bogey to head into the weekend 15 under and with a great chance of claiming the $4m (£3.05m) top prize.

"When I hit, after, I felt it was a little strong, but hit the pin and then went in," Kim said of her hole-in-one, the third of her career. "I think it was luck."

On the potential to win millions on Sunday, she added: "Money is money. It has not bothered me. I think winning is more important for me."

England's Charley Hull is one of six players four strokes back in a tie for third, with Jeeno Thitikul of Thailand one shot better off in second.

Hull posted a blemish-free 67, with five birdies, to keep herself right in the mix in a stacked field that contains the top 60 in this season's points list.

World number one Nelly Korda, who will qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame if she wins on Sunday, also produced a five-under 67 and heads into round three tied for 11th on nine under.

With an $11m purse on offer, Korda would also break Annika Sorenstam's career earnings record if she finishes in sixth place or better.

The Swede amassed 10 major titles and earned $22,583,694 during a storied career before retiring in 2008, with Korda now just under $160,000 behind that mark.

title: LPGA Tour: Charley Hull in CME Group Tour Championship contention as A Lim Kim fires hole-in-one to grab halfway lead
article_text:
A Lim Kim fired a hole-in-one on her way to grabbing the halfway lead at the LPGA Tour's season-ending CME Group Tour Championship, where Charley Hull remains in contention.

Kim holed her tee shot with a seven iron at the 168-yard par-three 16th, with the Korean adding seven birdies and a lone bogey in a round-of-the-day 64 at Tiburon Golf Club.

The former US Women's Open champion was tied at the top of the leaderboard until her stunning ace and a birdie at the par-five next, which moved Kim to 15 under and three clear of back-to-back defending champion Jeeno Thitikul.

Thitikul posted five birdies in a seven-hole stretch on her back nine during a second-round 67, putting her in the final group on Saturday, with Hull a further shot back in a share of third after matching the world No 2's score.

Yuri Yoshida, Ina Yoon, Yan Liu, Jenny Bae and Auston Kim complete the logjam on 11 under alongside Hull, who posted five birdies in a blemish-free round as the 2016 champion looks to win the CME Group Tour Championship for a second time.

"I've just been pretty solid the last couple days, and hopefully I can replicate that on the weekend," Hull admitted. "I didn't actually hole that many putts, but I hit it quite close."

Only the top 60 players in the season-long Race to the CME Globe get to tee it up in Florida, with world No 1 Nelly Korda six off the halfway lead as she chase the $4m (£3.04m) winner's cheque.

"I'm just not hitting it as solid as I would like," Korda explained. "I have a little bit of a two-way miss going and that's kind of death for any golfer - you're not very confident over the shot.

"I'm just trying to get myself one key that I'm just going to go with for the whole week. I have yet to figure it out - hopefully the weekend brings me some luck!"

England's Lottie Woad dropped to tied-22nd after a two-under 70, while Ireland's Leona Maguire heads into the weekend sharing 42nd after rounds of 70 and 71 over the first two days.

title: PGA Tour blasts LIV Golf creditors over 'desperate fishing expedition'
article_text:
The PGA Tour has launched a strong response to a legal move by creditors involved in LIV Golf's bankruptcy proceedings, branding their attempt to obtain sensitive business records a "desperate fishing expedition".

The comments came after the official committee of unsecured creditors in LIV Golf's Chapter 11 bankruptcy case issued a subpoena to the PGA Tour on Friday, requesting documents across 18 separate categories.

The PGA Tour has been asked to provide the material by December 4, with the demands covering everything from its relationship with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to financial information involving media rights, sponsorship agreements and player compensation.

However, the PGA Tour has made little secret of its frustration at being drawn into the proceedings.

"This document request is a desperate fishing expedition and a baseless attempt to try and drag the PGA Tour into the ongoing LIV Golf bankruptcy case," a Tour spokesperson told Front Office Sports.

"The efforts of these creditors should be dedicated towards LIV Golf and the parties responsible in the bankruptcy filing."

The latest development adds another twist to LIV Golf's increasingly complicated financial situation, following its November 5 announcement that it planned to wind down its operations.

Creditors have submitted more than $100 million in unsecured claims during the bankruptcy process, while LIV Golf has so far set aside $2 million for potential creditor recoveries, according to the information outlined in the proceedings.

The subpoena was filed by New Jersey-based law firm Fox Rothschild, representing the creditors committee alongside New York firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher.

Among the information being sought are documents connected to the previous litigation between the PGA Tour and LIV Golf, as well as communications concerning disciplinary action imposed or potentially considered against players who participated in, or explored joining, LIV events.

The creditors are also seeking records relating to the June 6, 2023 framework agreement involving the PGA Tour, DP World Tour and Saudi PIF.

Other areas of interest include communications concerning any arrangements or discussions that may have discouraged third parties from conducting business with LIV Golf, alongside documents connected to the US Department of Justice's inquiry into the proposed PGA Tour-PIF partnership.

Financial information is another significant part of the request, with the committee seeking details of the Tour's annual revenues, media-rights income, sponsorship earnings, tournament prize funds and overall player compensation.

Under bankruptcy legislation, creditors' committees have certain investigative powers allowing them to examine a debtor's financial affairs and business operations.

However, the subpoena does not automatically compel the PGA Tour to hand over every document requested. The organisation can challenge the demands or raise objections, potentially leaving the dispute to be considered by Judge Michael Kaplan, who is overseeing LIV Golf's bankruptcy case.

The next bankruptcy hearing is scheduled for November 24, with the latest dispute demonstrating that the fallout from LIV Golf's financial difficulties could extend well beyond the breakaway circuit itself.

title: PGA Tour: England's Marco Penge grabs halfway lead at RSM Classic as big names battle to secure FedExCup future
article_text:
England’s Marco Penge bolstered his hopes of retaining full status on the PGA Tour for next season by grabbing a share of the halfway lead at the RSM Classic.

Penge started the week 120th in the FedExCup standings and requiring at least a top-four finish to break inside the top 100 and guarantee full playing status on the PGA Tour in 2027.

A birdie-birdie finish saw Penge post a second-round 65 on the Stadium Course, one of two used at Sea Island Golf Club, leaving him in a four-way tie on nine under alongside Michael Thorbjornsen and Denmark's Rasmus Neergaard-Petersen.

"I'm in a bit of a weird situation," Penge admitted. "I missed seven or eight tournaments this year from injury and have some sort of medical exemption still, which I don't really know much about.

"I'm trying to feel like it's the last event, but at the same time knowing that I have maybe three or four, five tournaments to start next year that goes towards this year's ranking. There's a lot of us guys trying to keep our job this week and we're all trying to give it our all."

Thorbjornsen is already fully exempt on the PGA Tour next season, having won the Rocket Classic in August, while Neergaard-Petersen - like Penge - started the week outside the top 100 in the standings.

A congested leaderboard sees a further six players a shot back, including Ryder Cup player Rasmus Hojgaard as he looks to rise from 122 in the season standings, while England's Harry Hall heads into the weekend just two behind.

"It [FedExCup ranking] will always be in the back of your head a little bit," Hojgaard said. "There's still so much more golf to be played. I'm happy with the golf I played so far and hopefully I can keep doing that for the next few days."

Brooks Koepka, Presidents Cup star Jackson Koivun and past Ryder Cup captain Keegan Bradley are all four behind, while Christiaan Bezuidenhout - starting the week in 100th spot - is in tied-41st for the tournament and projected to drop down the standings.

A three-putt bogey on the final hole saw England's John Parry miss the cut by a shot, seeing him currently projected to finish in 101st spot, while eight-time PGA Tour winner Billy Horschel played his last three shots in four over and also made an early exit.

Those 51st to 60th after this week qualify for the first two Signature Events of 2027, while those who end between 101st and 125th on the PGA Tour only receive conditional status and be unable to feature in certain events.

Players outside the top 125 face a season on the Korn Ferry Tour or a trip to Q-School to earn their PGA Tour playing rights, with first-round leader Svensson entering the week in 135th spot.

title: DP World Tour winner questions controversial LIV Golf decision: 'It doesn't quite sit right with me'
article_text:
David Law believes players should have to earn their place on the DP World Tour, and he isn't entirely convinced by the decision to hand special invitations to multiple former LIV Golf stars for the 2027 season.

The 35-year-old Scot has welcomed the return of some of golf's biggest names, but believes offering opportunities to players without existing playing exemptions is a difficult decision to justify.

Having experienced first-hand just how difficult it can be to secure playing privileges on the European circuit, Law admits the latest arrangements don't quite sit right with him.

"The beauty of golf is that you have to earn everything you get," Law told GolfMagic.

"Giving players a large number of invites when they haven't gone through Q-School to earn their way onto our Tour doesn't quite sit right with me."

Law's comments come a week after the DP World Tour confirmed its membership arrangements for 2027, with nine former LIV Golf players set to receive tournament invitations after agreeing deals with the circuit.

Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith, Bubba Watson, Joaquin Niemann, Abraham Ancer, Carlos Ortiz, Thomas Pieters, Lucas Herbert and Michael La Sasso are among those who will receive opportunities to compete in selected regular DP World Tour events next season.

Two-time major champion Bryson DeChambeau has also taken up membership through an exemption earned by winning the 2024 US Open, while Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton have already made an immediate impact on their return, winning in Abu Dhabi and Dubai respectively.

They are not the only familiar faces returning to the European circuit, either.

Several other former LIV Golf stars have taken up DP World Tour membership through the career-money category, including Ryder Cup legends Sergio Garcia, Lee Westwood, Ian Poulter, Martin Kaymer, Graeme McDowell and Paul Casey.

South African trio Louis Oosthuizen, Charl Schwartzel and Branden Grace are also set to feature on the circuit next season.

There is little doubt that having players of that calibre back competing regularly in Europe will strengthen tournament fields and attract greater attention to the DP World Tour.

But not every member is convinced by the way some of those opportunities have been handed out.

Law was keen to make a distinction between the likes of Rahm and Hatton, who bring enormous value to the circuit, and those receiving special invitations without having earned playing privileges through the usual routes.

"I think it's fantastic for our Tour to have players like Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton playing full time in Europe. They are huge names and bring so much to our Tour," he said.

"I must admit I'm not a fan of handing out big numbers of invites to LIV players who aren't exempt, however."

It is a particularly interesting viewpoint given Law's own journey back to securing his place among Europe's elite.

The Aberdeen-born golfer, currently ranked No.297 in the Official World Golf Ranking, has experienced both the highs of winning on the DP World Tour and the uncertainty of fighting to keep his card.

Law worked his way through the Challenge Tour before earning promotion to the European Tour for the 2019 season, having won the SSE Scottish Hydro Challenge in 2018.

He then enjoyed a dream start to life on the top circuit, claiming his maiden DP World Tour title at the 2019 ISPS Handa Vic Open in Australia.

Law produced a stunning finish to win by one stroke, birdieing the 16th before eagling the final hole to complete a memorable comeback.

However, the Scot has since experienced a very different side of professional golf.

After losing his DP World Tour card at the end of 2024, Law fought his way back by winning twice on the HotelPlanner Tour in 2025.

But retaining his place for another season proved just as challenging.

A difficult 2026 campaign left Law needing a strong finish to avoid another spell outside the main circuit.

He responded by playing 11 consecutive events on the DP World Tour's Back 9, making eight cuts and climbing from 119th to 99th in the final Race to Dubai standings.

It was enough to squeeze him inside the all-important top 100 and secure his playing privileges for 2027.

"Getting back into Category 10 makes planning for 2027 much easier, and while I was hoping for more from my 2026 season, if you offered me 99th spot in the Race to Dubai with two months to go, I'd have taken it."

Law knows better than most that life on the DP World Tour can be unforgiving, particularly when results aren't going your way.

Having previously experienced the excitement of winning, he admits the pressure of fighting to retain a card is an entirely different proposition.

"It's a completely different kind of pressure," he explained.

"If you're up there at the right end of leaderboards, it's an exciting pressure and you're playing great, so you've got loads of control of your game.

"When you're battling to keep your card, it's because you've not been playing well, so that adds pressure in itself when you're out there competing."

The debate surrounding the returning LIV players also comes at an important time for the DP World Tour, which is looking to strengthen its tournaments and attract greater attention following a turbulent period for professional golf.

Chief executive Guy Kinnings has described the return of former LIV players as a major opportunity, particularly during periods when many of the circuit's leading dual members are competing in the United States.

title: Patrick Reed is back on the PGA Tour. This time he's not fighting demons
article_text:
On your list of prominent, major-winning American PGA Tour golfers thinking about going LIV, Patrick Reed had to be about dead last, right alongside Tiger Woods. Right? We’re talking about Captain America, with his drumstick forearms and swaggery, toes-out walk. Yes, ole Pat Reed. He’s only 36, but he married young, had kids young and has always seemed mature beyond his years, except when he hasn’t.

Reed, born in Texas in 1990, was raised on TW (Tiger Woods), George W. (Bush) — and red meat. The main course at the Masters dinner Reed hosted in 2019 was prime bone-in cowboy rib eye, if that means anything to you. He has been known to fly freshly cut steaks into remote tournament sites. For years, he wore black-and-red on tourney Sundays, à la Tiger.

In his 20s, as a card-carrying Tour player, you’d see P. Reed parading through your better American country-club clubhouses in custom-made cowboy boots. He secured his Tour playing privileges by getting through six Monday qualifiers (unheard of) in a four-month period in 2012, his future wife, Justine Karain, often caddying for him. Talk about earning it and keeping it in the family. Justine’s brother, Kessler Karain, has been Reed’s caddie for most of his career, including this year, when he had top-12 finishes in the Masters and the PGA Championship. One of Karain’s responsibilities is to make sure a particular and properly folded American flag is neatly tucked away in Reed’s golf bag, no matter the bag or occasion.

This is the guy who went LIV, signing for millions of guaranteed petrodollars by way of the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund?

Reed announced that he was departing for LIV in June 2022, shortly before the U.S. Open. He announced his departure from LIV, and his return to the PGA Tour, in late January 2026. He didn’t know then that the Saudi funding of the upstart golf league was about to evaporate. He did know that after playing the world for three and a half years, he missed home and his home tour. He missed 72-hole, full-field events with a cut. And he missed the adrenaline rush of PGA Tour golf, playing on a Sunday afternoon with a CBS or NBC camera in your face. He will now be back on the PGA Tour next season, having served his suspension and earned his card via the DP World Tour’s Race to Dubai.

Reed has been playing abroad, and off network TV, for so long now that casual golf fans may be surprised to learn he’s ranked solidly in the top 40 in the world (currently 33rd), and even that shorthand understates how good his golf is. There’s no quit in him, and his swing is a study in arms-to-body connectedness. In other words, it repeats. We’re likely to see a lot of Patrick Reed over the next decade or so, at the four majors, at the Players Championship and other sparkly Tour events and possibly during the most celebrated team events. Could he represent the United States in team events again? For sure.

“When I left the Tour and joined LIV, it was the right thing for me and my family,” Reed said earlier this spring. Actually, he said pretty much the same thing several times, over the course of several interviews. “I really enjoyed my time with LIV. I enjoyed playing all over the world, seeing all these different cultures. But now I’m super excited to be returning to the PGA Tour and ending my career where it began.”

It sounded like a practiced sound bite. It had to be a practiced sound bite. And the statement was surely true, as far as it went. It just didn’t go that far.

The deeper truth is sensitive and complicated and Reed won’t discuss it, at least not publicly, but it explains a great deal.

Reed’s life as a professional golfer is starting to look like a movie in three acts. Everyone who follows golf closely remembers Act I: Reed as a prominent PGA Tour player (nine wins) and repeated on-course rules issues that resulted in criticism on Golf Channel, whispering on Tour and a lot of pointed commentary from golf fans thumbing away, fast and furious, on their favorite social-media platforms. Reed could maybe have handled all that — he has an us-against-the-world mentality. But when his young daughter and son were mocked at school by mean-spirited kids mimicking what they heard at home — Yer dad’s a cheater — Reed decided to take his talents to LIV Golf.

Fewer people saw Act II: Reed as a globetrotting LIV Golf golfer, when, one prominent LIV official told me, Reed was a “perfect gentleman, a pleasure to be with, with no rules issues.” But if Reed took ownership for any of his various rule book episodes, nobody I talked to knew anything about it. Now comes Act III: Reed’s return, possibly with more people watching than ever before.

Reed told me, in a firm and civil tone, that he didn’t want to revisit his past. (I had brought up two rules events, one in 2019 at Tiger’s Hero World Challenge, where Reed was contending; the other at the 2021 Farmers Insurance Open, which Reed won.) I asked him if he had regrets, if there were things he had done for which he’d like a mulligan. No, in a word. “I believe everything happens for a purpose,” Reed said. “Everything in my life, from the time I was born, right through this interview, happens for a reason.” Happens for a reason. He’s not the first person in the history of mankind to cite the phrase.

Jesper Svensson catches fire late to seize early lead at The RSM Classic
article_text:
ST. SIMONS ISLAND, Ga. (AP) — Michael Thorbjornsen spent the last few weeks working on his iron play and saw it pay off Thursday in the rain and wind at Sea Island. He made five of his seven birdies inside 10 feet for a 6-under 64 and the low score on the Seaside Course to trail Sweden's Jesper Svensson, who played the Plantation Course, by two shots at The RSM Classic.

Thorbjornsen, one of the group of rising young stars who won the Rocket Classic this year for his first PGA Tour title, had five birdies in a seven-hole stretch around the turn at the tougher Seaside Course (par 70), which included an 8-foot par save.

Michael Thorbjornsen's 146-yard approach sets up birdie on No. 11 at The RSM

Svensson, who needs at least a two-way tie for second to finish among the top 100 in the FedExCup to keep a full card for next year, birdied his last four holes on the easier Plantation Course (par 72) for an 8-under 64. He entered the week No. 135 in the FedExCup standings.

The final tournament of the PGA Tour season brings different levels of pressure, mainly for those who want to be fully exempt next year by finishing in the top 100.

“Everybody knows what they need to do out there,” Grillo said after a 66 at Plantation. “Yeah, good start. Hopefully many more of these. I know what I need to do and it was good.”

Thorbjornsen is among nine players in the field who finished in the top 50 on the PGA Tour and are exempt for all of the $20 million Signature Events in 2027. He felt the missing piece was his iron game, not giving himself enough birdie chances.

“We've worked very hard on my irons, just having more control,” Thorbjornsen said. “My driving stats have been pretty decent these past couple years and I haven’t really been able to take advantage of it. So trying to get the ball closer to the hole. That gives you more birdie looks but also less bogey chances.”

Ten of the top 16 players on the leaderboard to par came into the week outside the top 100 in the FedExCup standings. Thirty-five spots outside of the magic number, Svensson spent most of his day trying to keep himself and his golf clubs dry and negotiating a wind that wasn't as strong as practice rounds but no less a nuisance.

The Swede had seven birdies on the back nine at Plantation and only wants to keep going.

“You can’t really deny the situation that you’re in,” Svensson said. “Not really thinking of it when you’re playing as much as trying to hit the right areas and hit some good shots. That’s number one task really and see where that takes me.”

Brooks Koepka has been working with new coaches, including Brad Faxon with his putting that hurt him so much this year. Playing for the first time in six weeks, the five-time major champion opened with a 67 on Seaside.

Brooks Koepka holes 59-foot shot for birdie on No. 14 at The RSM

Blades Brown, at No. 54 in the world and hopeful of a late push to get into the Masters by the end of the year, had a pair of birdies late in his round to salvage a 1-under 69 at Seaside. Ben James, the PGA Tour University's No. 1 player in 2026 who is one spot behind Brown in the world ranking, shot 4-under 68 at Plantation.

Thorbjornsen and Mitchell head to the easier Plantation on Friday. They were the only players in the top 10 on the leaderboard who played Seaside in the opening round.

title: England's Hull one stroke off lead at lucrative LPGA finale
article_text:
England's Charley Hull carded a six-under-par 66 to sit one shot off the first-round lead at the LPGA's lucrative season-ending CME Group Tour Championship.

Australia's Karis Davidson, South Korea's Kim A-lim and Thailand's Jeeno Thitikul, set the pace at seven under at the Tiburon Golf Club in Naples, Florida.

World number two Thitikul, who is aiming to win the event for the third consecutive season, responded to a bogey on the 12th hole by knocking in five consecutive birdies on the back nine.

Hull, who triumphed a decade ago, is one of nine players a stroke behind the leading trio on a stacked leaderboard that contains the top 60 in this season's points list, who are all chasing the $4m (£3.05m) top prize.

"When I won 10 years ago I didn't really take golf seriously. I remember coming into this event when I won, hungover," Hull said.

"I felt pretty good [today]. I kind of like lost my swing feels [at the] end of last week because my hip was very tight, and it just like started rerouting my golf swing," Hull said.

"Today I was nervous on the first tee. I felt like I had no swing feeling. Then as the round developed I felt like I hit it really nice."

Hull's compatriot Lottie Woad made six birdies and a bogey as she signed for five-under 67, along with France's Celine Boutier.

World number one Nelly Korda, who will qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame if she wins on Sunday, endured a mixed day but picked up shots on the 17th and 18th as she finished on four under.

With an $11m purse on offer, Korda would also break Annika Sorenstam's career earnings record if she finishes in sixth place or better.

The Swede amassed 10 major titles and earned $22,583,694 during a storied career before retiring in 2008, with Korda now just under $160,000 behind that mark.

title: RSM Classic: Billy Horschel faces setback over PGA Tour future after slow start, as Jesper Svensson races ahead
article_text:
Sweden's Jesper Svensson holds a one-shot lead after the opening round of the RSM Classic, the final PGA Tour event of the season; Brooks Koepka is five strokes back and Billy Horschel is seven behind; watch the second round live on Friday from 1.30pm on Sky Sports Golf

Jesper Svensson produced a late burst to grab the early lead at the RSM Classic, as Billy Horschel made a slow start to his bid to retain full PGA Tour playing rights.

Only the top 100 in the FedExCup standings after this week's event in St Simons Island remain fully exempt on the PGA Tour, with Horschel heading into the week 101st and projected to fall further down the rankings after opening with a one-under 71.

Horschel - an eight-time winner on the PGA Tour - carded three birdies and two bogeys on the Plantation Course, one of two used at Sea Island Golf Club, to leave him seven strokes behind Svensson.

Svensson birdied eight of his last 11 holes on the same course as Horschel - including each of his last four - to post an eight-under 64 and move into a one-shot lead, with Max Greyserman and Garrick Higgo sharing second after opening 65s.

Michael Thorbjornsen posted the lowest round on the Seaside Course, with a six-under 64 leaving him tied-fourth alongside Emiliano Grillo, Hank Lebioda, Maverick McNealy, Lee Hodges and Davis Riley.

Ramsus Hojgaard and Marco Penge, entering the week outside the top 100 in the season-long standings, sit in the group on four under alongside Ryder Cup player Sepp Straka - who finished inside top 50 during the regular season.

Koepka described his season as a "disappointment" ahead of this week's event, with the five-time major champion opening with a three-under 67, while England's John Parry - entering the week 96th in the ranking - started with a two-under 70.

All players ranked No 51 and below carry their FedExCup points over from the regular season and first play-off event into the 'FedExCup Fall', giving them the chance to boost their status for next season.

Those 51st to 60th after this week qualify for the first two Signature Events of 2027, while those who end between 101st and 125th on the PGA Tour only receive conditional status and be unable to feature in certain events.

Players outside the top 125 face a season on the Korn Ferry Tour or a trip to Q-School to earn their PGA Tour playing rights, with first-round leader Svensson entering the week in 135th spot.

title: Here’s the prize money payout for each golfer at the LPGA’s 2026 CME Group Tour Championship
article_text:
Just like on the PGA Tour, the LPGA season is ending this week. But, unlike what’s happening up in Georgia, $4 million will go to the winner of the CME Group Tour Championship. The total purse is $11 million at Tiburon Golf Club in Naples, with the biggest winner’s check on tour going to the first-place finisher.

Nelly Korda and Jeeno Thitikul, World Nos. 1 and 2, are the ones to beat, but winning multiple times this season. Korda, however, won two majors while Thitikul is still looking for her first. However, she is the two-time defending champion this week after winning each of the last two years.

Korda, like last week, has another chance at earning entrance into the LPGA’s Hall of Fame. Only a victory will get here there.

The 60-player field is made up of 17 of the 19 winners on tour this season. That includes Lindy Duncan, a popular first-time winner last week at the Annika Sorenstam event outside Tampa. In all, there are 20 of the top 25 players in the world competing.

title: What to make of Tiger Woods' return to golf at Hero World Classic, Bryson DeChambeau's move to DP World Tour
article_text:
The DP World Tour's 2027 season came to end this past weekend with Rory McIlroy claiming the Race to Dubai and Tyrrell Hatton running away with the DP World Tour Championship. Hatton's victory came one week after his former LIV Golf mate, Jon Rahm, won the Abu Dhabi Championship as the reassimilation of those who left the European circuit only to return a few years later is well underway.

It is not just Europeans, however, who are flocking to the DP World Tour, but also Bryson DeChambeau. News surfaced Tuesday that he has The inclusion of these players will beef up the DP World Tour next season, but is there another angle we should consider?

The PGA Tour wraps up its season this weekend at the RSM Classic in Sea Island, Georgia, while Tiger Woods will begin a new season of his career next month at the Hero World Challenge. Will this comeback be any different, or should we frame it in a new light given his off-the-course issues?

The game keeps moving, and CBS Sports is keeping up with it as we dive into the most pressing issues and conversation points with the newest edition of The Three Putt.

After winning his eighth Race to Dubai crown, McIlroy mentioned how difficult it will be to repeat (again) in 2027. Well, lo and behold, the gates of LIV Golf have brought a flood of former and new members to the DP World Tour with DeChambeau leading the charge.

Following years of carrying the water for LIV Golf, DeChambeau will be able to access any tournament of his choosing on the DP World Tour next season thanks to his 2024 U.S Open win. What do you think of the move at large?

Robby Kalland: It was really his only play, so it's not surprising, but I am extremely intrigued by what the DP World Tour can be next year. The challenge the DP World Tour has faced in recent years is that their best players defect to the PGA Tour every year, with the top 10 all earning cards. Next year, they are going to have their usual crop plus an influx of LIV stars waiting out their year-long suspension from returning to the PGA Tour (barring a sudden change of heart from the bosses in Ponte Vedra).

DeChambeau, Rahm, Hatton & Co. will suddenly be tournament staples. We've already seen Rahm and Hatton win this fall, and Patrick Reed dominated early in 2026 after leaving LIV Golf. Will we see DeChambeau, Rahm and Hatton all collect trophies in 2027? Will there be a bit more parity than expected on the international circuit? These are some outstanding questions.

Patrick McDonald: All of this comes at such an interesting time. The PGA Tour and DP World Tour are deep in negotiations regarding the new strategic alliance ahead of changes coming in 2028. One point of contention appears to be how many cards will be awarded to the top finishers on the DP World Tour; four is rumored to be the magic number for the Championship Series.

It feels safe to say players like Hatton and Niemann (depending on how many starts the latter gets) will contend for those, leaving just a couple for the DP World Tour faithful. All of this to say, yes, the LIV alumni should play well, win trophies, grow the game in the far corners of the world and put the last five years behind them, but the trickle-down effects from this move could be more compelling.

One man we know won't be competing on the DP World Tour next year is Tiger, but the Big Cat is making his return next month at his event in the Bahamas, the Hero World Challenge. We haven't seen Woods play outdoor golf since 2024, and he's had more surgeries (and more off-course trouble) since then. What are your expectations for Tiger's latest comeback, and how differently do you feel about this return compared to others?

McDonald: I swear we are stuck in a "Groundhog Day"-like time loop; we are always left talking about Tiger and a potential comeback this time of year. His game is gone when stacked against Scottie Scheffler and the lot, but the major schedule has to motivate him for 2027 with stops at Pebble Beach and St. Andrews on the docket. Beyond that, he has to be eyeing the all-time USGA championship record, as he is tied with Bobby Jones for the most all-time with nine.

If that is his North Star, and he is competing against the olds, I am more optimistic than the song and dance of the last five or so years, which has been tough to watch and sometimes sad to follow. What say you?

Kalland: Last year was the first of my life that neither Tiger nor Phil Mickelson played in a major, and at the risk of getting excommunicated from the golf writer world ... dare I say ... it was borderline refreshing?

Those two defined golf for so long, and when it was what they were doing on the golf course, the sport was arguably the best it's ever been. Unfortunately, that duo has produced far more headlines for controversies off of it recently, and the dominant feeling for me around Woods' latest return is best described as trepidation.

I hope it works out. I hope his body can hold up. I hope this latest DUI and rollover car crash was a legitimate wake-up call for him to get a better handle on things. However, the entire time, we'll all be wondering when the other shoe will drop -- whether with an injury or something else that happens away from the course.

title: PGA Tour winner misses crucial opportunity after injury forces season-ending exit
article_text:
Two-time PGA Tour winner Erik van Rooyen will not earn conditional status for the 2027 season after being forced to withdraw from the final event of the season with injury.

The big South African pulled out of the RSM Classic on Thursday morning because of a rib injury, the PGA Tour confirmed.

Six-time Tour winner Bill Haas was drafted into the field at Sea Island Resort as his replacement.

Van Rooyen had entered the tournament with hopes of improving his position in the FedExCup Fall standings and securing conditional status for next season.

The 34-year-old had enjoyed an encouraging run of form in recent weeks, recording top-10 finishes in two of his previous three starts, including a tie for fourth at last week's Austin Championship.

Those results lifted him to 125th in the points standings, putting him in contention to secure playing opportunities for 2027.

However, his withdrawal means he is now projected to miss out on conditional status, dealing a significant blow to his hopes of retaining playing privileges on the PGA Tour.

Haas, meanwhile, was a late replacement after an eventful week of travel.

The American had attempted to qualify for the tournament through Monday's qualifier but finished one shot outside a play-off for the final two available places.

Golf Channel reported that Haas made a five-hour drive home, only to be informed that a space in the field was on offer at the last minute.

He made the journey back to south Georgia on Wednesday and was confirmed as a replacement for Van Rooyen, giving him the opportunity to make just his third PGA Tour appearance of the year.

The RSM Classic is the final tournament of the PGA Tour's fall schedule.

More than a dozen changes had already been made to the field since Monday, with the late withdrawal of Van Rooyen providing another reminder of the uncertainty surrounding the tournament's line-up.

Former champion Ludvig Aberg was among those to withdraw. The Swede tweaked his back, but a subsequent MRI scan revealed no serious damage had been done.

Several big names are in danger of losing full status for the 2027 season.

Only the top 100 players in the rankings earn full cards.

Billy Horschel, Marco Penge, Joel Dahmen and former U.S. Open champion Lucas Glover are among the notables in danger of losing full status.

title: Darcy Graham lifts lid on injury and why he's 'glad' he made decision he did
article_text:
Darcy Graham acknowledged he could easily have been looking in from the outside instead of basking in the after-glow of his fifth Scotland hat-trick.

Edinburgh head coach Sean Everitt revealed in September that the prolific wing was set to be out until Christmas with a bicep problem sustained in a pre-season friendly.

But a few weeks later it emerged that Graham and his club had opted to go down the rehabilitation route rather than surgery, and the 29-year-old was able to return to action last month, paving the way for him to be involved in Gregor Townsend’s Nations Championship squad.

After playing his part in last weekend’s hard-fought 15-12 win over Australia, Graham notched a treble in Saturday’s 67-5 rout of Japan, taking his tally for Scotland to 41 tries and moving him six clear of clubmate Duhan van der Merwe at the top of the national team’s all-time scoring charts.

“I actually said to the physio before the game I’m glad we went the non-surgical route on that bicep, as I wouldn’t have been here (otherwise), I would have been out until Christmas time,” Graham said.

“That Glasgow game (on December 27) was my return to play, so my season could have looked very different.

“If you can keep away from the operation table, it’s definitely better to do that. We had that two-week period to try and see how my arm coped with training and playing. It coped really well, so I’m delighted.”

That reprieve has allowed Graham, who has been beset by injuries in recent season, to set about reasserting himself in Scotland’s back three after losing his status as a guaranteed starter at the beginning of this year’s Six Nations.

“The competition in the Scotland team now is just through the roof, especially in the back-three positions, with Kyle Rowe, Jamie Dobie and Kyle Steyn playing unbelievable through at Glasgow, they’re carving it up every week,” said Graham.

“For myself, I need to keep pushing. It’s probably easy getting back to where I was but the hard part is staying at that level. I’ve just got to keep working away, keeping hammering away at training and showing what I can do.”

The Scots will wrap up their inaugural Nations Championship campaign against Argentina at Allianz Stadium in London next Sunday after finishing fourth in the northern hemisphere table with four wins and two defeats against the heavyweights of South Africa and New Zealand.

“That New Zealand game was obviously frustrating,” said Graham. “I don’t think we really showed what we were about.

“And then we never really got going again in the Australia game so it was just nice to go out and put a real attacking performance out there (against Japan), especially as a backline, to be able to go out and do what we’re good at.”

title: Daniil Medvedev downplays Alexander Zverev’s improvement after ATP Finals defeat
article_text:
Alexander Zverev is one win away from completing his perfect season after he stormed into the championship match at the ATP Finals with a win against Daniil Medvedev.

Zverev recorded his 69th win of a year that has seen him win his first two Grand Slam titles at the Roland Garros and the US Open, with his 7-6(0), 6-4 win over Medvedev in Turin giving him a shot at Carlos Alcaraz in the final.

The newly crowned world No 1 has been frustrated by constant suggestions that he has only claimed the world No 1 ranking due to long-term injuries afflicting Jannik Sinner and Alcaraz.

Medvedev had a 14-8 winning record against Zverev prior to their latest meeting, so he is perfectly placed to give a verdict on whether the German has raised his level over the last year.

Zverev did not face a break point in the two sets against Medvedev, with his opponent suggesting his biggest weapon will always be his serve.

“I think his serve is better,” declared Medvedev, before he was asked if Zverev’s forehand has also gone up a level and he replied: “I will put it this way: I think his forehand was very good even before, and then sometimes he can miss. Today he also missed a couple, so I would not say it’s better.

“I said even before the match, serve is important. Actually, probably Sascha didn’t get broken yet this tournament, so not easy. Didn’t get a break point, so of course not that easy.

“On the tiebreak, I had to do a bit better if I wanted to win the set, and same on the second set when I got broken. Could have done maybe a little bit better. But deserved to lose, so we move on.”

Zverev will be desperate to record a win against Alcaraz and banish the notion that he is a step behind what some have claimed are the real ‘Big 2’ in men’s tennis, with former world No 1 Jim Courier among those admitting outside factors will always cloud some judgements on the German.

Back in June 2024, criminal proceedings against Zverev over allegations he pushed and strangled his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea, were discontinued by a Berlin court following a settlement.

Zverev denied the accusations, and court proceedings ended without a verdict or a finding of guilt. Under the agreement, Zverev was ordered to pay €150,000 to the German state and a further €50,000 to charitable organisations.

In an interview with L’Equipe after his Roland Garros victory in June, Zverev said the allegations against him “have been proven false” and that his “innocence has been proven”.

According to Bounces, Patea has filed a new civil lawsuit against Zverev over alleged ‘false statements’ made in that L’Equipe interview, with Courier arguing those allegations will always haunt Zverev.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

“Well, the computer is the computer. It doesn’t have any feelings. It just spits out the numbers on who did what,” he said on a recent episode of the Off Court with Greg Rusedski podcast as he spoke about the debate over Zverev’s rise to the world No 1 ranking.

“He’s the most accomplished tennis player this year. He’s got the most points in the last 52 weeks and there he’s the 30th person to have that honour. So yes, he’s earned it. And anyone who doesn’t think that it is just not using their analytical or critical mind. They’re using their emotions.

“And people have strong feelings about Zverev because of all the on-court issues, off-court issues that he’s dealt with over his career that has made it a little more complicated, I think, for some people to to watch his career.

“If you just look at his performance, two major titles, he’s been ultra consistent, and he is the world number one. And I don’t think it’s disputable that the computer is what it is and the ranking is what it is.”
